newsitem.title: USA: Florida OKs chemical castration for sex offenders.
newsitem.headline: Florida OKs chemical castration for sex offenders.

text.p: A new Florida law requiring chemical castration of convicted rapists should act as a deterrent but may not be used for some time, officials said Friday.

Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles Thursday let stand a bill that requires repeat sexual offenders to be treated with the drug medroxyprogesterone acetate, known as MPA. The law, which will apply to anyone convicted of sexual battery after Oct. 1, is similar to one passed in California last year.
Backers, who spent years battling for approval of the law, say the treatment is effective and will substantially reduce repeat offences in a crime known for its high recidivism rate.

"I think it will act as a deterrent," said Representative Mark Ogles, a Bradenton Republican and a sponsor of the bill. "The stakes are pretty high if they know they are going to jail and when they get out they are either going to have physical or chemical castration for virtually the rest of their lives."
Florida is one of a handful of states to adopt a chemical castration statute. California's law, which went into effect Jan. 1, has yet to be used.

Florida corrections officials say the bill will not have an immediate impact. Before a chemical castration could take place, a sexual offender must be caught, convicted, sentenced under the new law and exhaust all appeals.

"Hopefully we won't see it for a while. They will have plenty of options to appeal and it may take a few years," said Peggy Ball, legislative director for the department. "My guess is that by and large judges will use them in the most horrendous cases. Not on the average case."

Critics say the treatment constitutes cruel and unusual punishment. Similar techniques including sterilisation and lobotomies were used on inmates and the disabled through the early part of the 20th century, said opponent Larry Spaulding, spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union.
"We haven't done that in a half-century primarily because the U.S. Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional," he said.

Spaulding also said the procedures may not work. "The use of the drug on a voluntary basis combined with intensive counselling has proven to be reasonably successful for individuals who want to be helped," he said.
"There is no empirical evidence that forced use of drugs is going to cure anybody."

Under the new law, judges would be allowed to include MPA treatment as part of their sentences for first-time offenders. On a second conviction, the judge would be required to order chemical castration. Under both scenarios, the defendant could opt for physical castration instead.
